title: Roosevelt Island - Manhattan Healing Forest
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded in the Manhattan Healing Forest, our survey station is Roosevelt Island’s Southpoint Park, beginning June 24, 2026. This data was last updated August 4, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Eastern Red Bats and Hoary Bats: NYC’s Migratory Bats of the Summer
Roosevelt Island’s most common species is the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis), which makes up the vast majority of our bat detections at this site (depicted in the graph above in green). This is the most common bat in most of New York City throughout the summer. We also see a very small number of hoary bats (Lasiurus cinereus), an uncommon local species, on Roosevelt Island. If you look close, you can see a golden yellow sliver that starts around August 2nd, this indicates hoary bat numbers have started to pick up with the beginning of August.
Though both of these species live in New York City throughout the summer, they are migratory and will head south as temperatures begin to drop in the fall. The early August increase in hoary bat activity could represent a migratory wave of bats passing through NYC on their way to their wintering destinations.



Eastern Red Bat



Hoary Bat




About iDig2Learn and the Manhattan Healing Forest, our community partners on Roosevelt Island
Our community partner and liaison with the Roosevelt Island Operating Corporation is Christina Delfico, the main organizing force behind the Manhattan Healing Forest and the community nature initiative, iDig2Learn. The Manhattan Healing Forest is New York State’s first Miyawaki Method Pocket Forest. Roughly the size of a tennis court, it contains tight knit plantings of 1,500 native trees and shrubs in Southpoint Park. Forest funding partners SUGi and leaders from the Lenape Center and Yakama Nation helped plant forty-seven native plant species in April 202. In addition to bats, this small forest corner of Roosevelt Island is also home to kestrels, hawks, falcons, Monarch butterflies and native bees.

title: McCarren Demonstration Garden at McCarren Park - Williamsburg, BK
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at the McCarren Demonstration Garden in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. This garden was the site of a bat rescue earlier this summer and we began monitoring on June 6, 2026. This data was last updated August 4, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Eastern Red Bats: A flexible species
The two most commonly detected species at the McCarren Demonstration Garden are the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis) and big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus). You can see by the alternating colors above that they regularly fluctuate in terms of who is more common.
Red bats are very nomadic, moving their home every one to two days, and flexible in the type of habitat they are willing to use. In the challenging landscape of New York City, this can be a strength. McCarren Park is a great example of this. Though it is far from fresh water and larger, forested parks, red bats are still able to find and take refuge in McCarren Park’s limited habitat. Keep an eye on the baseball lights nearby during the summer and you may even see the occasional red bat feeding off the bugs they attract.



Eastern Red Bat



Big Brown Bat




About McCarren Park Demonstration Garden
We first began working with McCarren Park Demonstration Garden when they invited our principal ecologist, Nic, to give a talk about urban bats in 2025. After a pregnant red bat was discovered hiding in their planting beds earlier this summer, we set up a monitoring station in the garden. From their website:
The McCarren Park Demonstration Garden is an initiative of North Brooklyn Mutual Aid and GrowNYC. We’re a space for environmental education and climate justice, and we’re so happy you’re here.
There are no individual plots in our garden—we grow everything together. We focus on food and flowers to stock our local free fridges. In 2024, we harvested 935 lbs of produce for our neighbors! We also provide free workshops and events for the community, and a chance to make new friends while getting your hands a little dirty.

title: GrowNYC Teaching Garden at Governor’s Island
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at the GrowNYC Teaching Garden on Governor’s Island, a small island just south of Manhattan. We began monitoring bat activity on May 13, 2026. This data was last updated August 5, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










A Stop Over for All of our Local Bat Species
While most of our parks within NYC tend to be dominated by our two most common species, you can see on the graph above that Governor’s Island hosts a significant amount of activity from all four: eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis), big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus), silver-haired bat (Lasionycteris noctivagans), and hoary bat (Lasiurus cinereus). This coastal habitat may be especially easy for migrating bats to spot, but for now we can only speculate as to why Governor’s Island hosts such diversity.



Eastern Red Bat



Big Brown Bat


 Hoary Bat


 Silver-haired Bat




About the GrowNYC Teaching Garden on Governor’s Island
As we prepared to wrap up our research season in 2025, we received a message on Instagram about a bat visiting some fig trees on Governor’s Island. Intrigued, we began chatting with the farmer that submitted the observation and GrownNYC’s teaching garden on the island became a top priority site for monitoring this year.



An eastern red bat sleeps in a fig tree on Governor’s Island. Photo by Jules White


Our primary contact on the island is farmer, law student, bird watcher, and bicycling wonder, Jules White. Jules has been an amazing supporter of Urban Bat Project, helping with the Governor’s Island surveys and our winter research in Green-Wood Cemetery. From GrowNYC’s website:
The GrowNYC Teaching Garden on Governors Island is a one-acre urban farm that aims to engage, excite, and educate New Yorkers in all aspects of urban farming and food. We hosts K-12 field trips, public workshops, and donate excess produce we grow to NYC partners from May to October. Discover the power of urban farming, fresh food, and climate action by planning your next visit!



Our local partner, Jules White, in front of the Teaching Garden

title: Greenway Botanical Garden at the Naval Cemetery Landscape - Williamsburg, BK
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at the Botanical Garden at Naval Cemetery Landscape in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. This is our second year working with the Brooklyn Greenway Initiative at this site, with this year’s surveys beginning on May 29, 2026. This data was last updated July 11, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Big Brown Bats and Eastern Red Bats: Two Very Different Approaches to NYC
The two most commonly detected species at the Naval Cemetery Landscape are the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis) and big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus). You can see by the alternating colors above that they regularly fluctuate in terms of who is more common.
Eastern red bats are nomadic, migratory bats that spend the summer in NYC. They typically move to a new location every 1-2 days and are extremely flexible in their habitat requirements. Big brown bats, on the other hand, are very particular about finding the best quality habitat available. Once they’ve found a spot they like, they’ll make it their home until its time for them to hibernate in the winter.



Eastern Red Bat



Big Brown Bat




About the Brooklyn Greenway Initiative and the Botanical Garden at Naval Cemetery Landscape
Brooklyn Greenway Initiative is the team behind the restoration of Naval Cemetery Landscape. We began working with them in 2025 and they have been incredible partners in research. In 2026, we began offering bat walks at this location. From their website:
Brooklyn Greenway Initiative built the Naval Cemetery Landscape (now called the Greenway Botanical Garden at the Naval Cemetery) in 2016 on the site of the former Naval Hospital Cemetery at the Brooklyn Navy Yard as a place for retreat and remembrance while honoring its rich layers of natural and cultural history. This site was designed as a native plant meadow and pollinator habitat, and provides visitors with an escape from urban life. Many rare birds and insects can be seen here. There are magnifying glasses on site and visitors are encouraged to bring their own binoculars to observe the bird species from the boardwalk
